title: Freshness, Citations, Abstention & RAG Cost
scopeHtml: Scope: Making updates searchable, verifying citations, knowing when not to answer, and costing ingestion/retrieval/generation.

notes.title: Why freshness, citations, abstention and cost belong together
notes.html:
A RAG system (retrieval-augmented generation: look up documents, paste the best ones into the prompt, let the model answer from them) looks finished once the demo works. Production breaks it in four quiet ways, and this note covers all four:

  1. Stale answers. The policy document changed on Monday, but the index still holds last month's chunks, so the bot confidently quotes the old rule.
  2. Fake or unsupported citations. The answer ends with "[Source: HR-Policy.pdf, p. 4]", but page 4 does not say that. The citation is decoration, not evidence.
  3. Answering when it should not. The question is outside the knowledge base, or retrieval returned junk, and the model still produces a fluent, wrong answer.
  4. A bill nobody can explain. Finance asks "what does one answer cost?" and the team has only the total from the model provider.

Terms used throughout (defined once here):

  • Chunk: a slice of a document (for example 400 tokens) stored as one searchable unit.
  • Embedding: a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a chunk; similar meanings give nearby vectors.
  • Index / vector store: the database holding chunks, vectors and metadata (pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, OpenSearch, FAISS).
  • Token: a piece of text (roughly 3 to 4 English characters) that models read and bill by.
  • Grounded answer: an answer whose claims are supported by the retrieved text.
 documents change --> [ingest] --> index --> [retrieve] --> [generate + cite]
        ^                 |                      |                 |
   freshness SLO     idempotent upsert     confidence gate    citation verify
                          |                      |                 |
                          +------ cost meter on every stage -------+
                                                 |
                                       abstain if gate fails

Existing notes already cover related ground: see also 03_O1 (sections "Freshness and indexing operations" and "Cost and latency of RAG" give the short checklist version) and 01_R1 (ingestion basics). This note goes deeper: the exact mechanics of making an update searchable, the concrete algorithms for verifying a citation, how to choose an abstention threshold with data, and cost formulas with worked arithmetic.

Real-world anchors. Perplexity and Bing Chat style products show numbered citations next to each claim; Google's NotebookLM and Anthropic's citations feature (verify current API shape in the docs) return spans pointing back to source passages; enterprise copilots (Microsoft Copilot, Glean, Notion AI) are judged on how fast edited documents become searchable.

Real life. A newsroom archive assistant: it must know today's correction, show which clipping supports each sentence, say "not in our archive" when asked about something never printed, and report what each research request costs.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating these as separate features. They share one trace: the same retrieved chunks, scores and token counts feed freshness checks, citation checks, the abstention gate and the cost meter.
  • Saying "just use a bigger model" for hallucinations. A bigger model still cannot know a document that is not in the index, and still invents citations.
  • Forgetting that all four need numbers (lag in seconds, citation precision, abstention precision, dollars per answer) or they cannot be improved.

notes.title: Freshness: how an edit becomes searchable
notes.html:
Plain words. Freshness is the time between "someone changed the source of truth" and "the changed text can be retrieved". The system is only as fresh as the slowest step in the pipeline.

Why it is hard. Documents live in many places (Confluence, Google Drive, SharePoint, S3, a database, Git). Each reports changes differently, and embeddings are computed by a separate service, so an edit passes through several queues before it is searchable.

The pipeline, step by step.

source edit
   |  (1) detect change: webhook / change feed / polling diff
   v
queue (Kafka, SQS, Pub/Sub)         <- absorbs bursts, enables retries
   |  (2) fetch current content, compute content hash
   v
hash same as stored?  --yes--> stop (no cost)
   | no
   v  (3) parse + chunk
   v  (4) embed ONLY changed chunks
   v  (5) upsert new chunks, delete the stale ones (same doc_id)
   v
index refresh (the vector store makes it visible)   <- (6) often a delay!
   |
   v  (7) freshness probe confirms: query for a phrase from the new text

Numbers to reason with (illustrative, verify for your stack):

  • Webhook detection: seconds. Polling every 15 min: average lag 7.5 min, worst 15 min (poll interval P gives average P/2, worst P).
  • Embedding a batch of 100 chunks: roughly 1 to 3 seconds with a hosted API (verify).
  • Vector store visibility: pgvector is transactional (visible at commit); Elasticsearch/OpenSearch refresh interval defaults to 1 s; some managed stores are eventually consistent for seconds to minutes (verify per product).

Content hashing avoids re-embedding the world. Hash the normalized text of each chunk (SHA-256). If the hash equals the stored one, skip embedding. Embedding cost scales with changed text, not total corpus size. Worked example: corpus of 1,000,000 chunks, 2% changes per day, each chunk 400 tokens. Daily re-embed of changed chunks only = 20,000 x 400 = 8,000,000 tokens. Full re-embed = 1,000,000 x 400 = 400,000,000 tokens. Hashing is 50x cheaper (400M / 8M = 50).

Idempotent upsert. Give each chunk a deterministic id such as doc_id:chunk_index:hash8. Running the same job twice must produce the same index state, because queues deliver at-least-once.

import hashlib

def chunk_hash(text: str) -> str:
    norm = " ".join(text.split())          # collapse whitespace so reformatting is not a "change"
    return hashlib.sha256(norm.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

def sync_document(doc_id: str, new_chunks: list[str], store, embed):
    """store: has get_hashes(doc_id)->dict[int,str], upsert(items), delete(ids). embed: list[str]->list[vector]."""
    old = store.get_hashes(doc_id)                     # {chunk_index: hash}
    todo = [(i, c) for i, c in enumerate(new_chunks) if old.get(i) != chunk_hash(c)]
    if todo:
        vectors = embed([c for _, c in todo])          # only changed chunks are embedded
        store.upsert([
            {"id": f"{doc_id}:{i}", "vector": v, "hash": chunk_hash(c),
             "doc_id": doc_id, "text": c}
            for (i, c), v in zip(todo, vectors)
        ])
    stale = [f"{doc_id}:{i}" for i in old if i >= len(new_chunks)]   # doc got shorter
    if stale:
        store.delete(stale)
    return {"embedded": len(todo), "deleted": len(stale)}   # prints e.g. {'embedded': 2, 'deleted': 1}
import java.security.MessageDigest

fun chunkHash(text: String): String {
    val norm = text.trim().split(Regex("\\s+")).joinToString(" ")
    return MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(norm.toByteArray())
        .joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }
}

interface Store {
    fun getHashes(docId: String): Map<Int, String>
    fun upsert(items: List<Map<String, Any>>)
    fun delete(ids: List<String>)
}

fun syncDocument(docId: String, newChunks: List<String>, store: Store, embed: (List<String>) -> List<FloatArray>): Pair<Int, Int> {
    val old = store.getHashes(docId)
    val todo = newChunks.withIndex().filter { (i, c) -> old[i] != chunkHash(c) }
    if (todo.isNotEmpty()) {
        val vectors = embed(todo.map { it.value })
        store.upsert(todo.mapIndexed { n, (i, c) ->
            mapOf("id" to "$docId:$i", "vector" to vectors[n], "hash" to chunkHash(c), "doc_id" to docId, "text" to c)
        })
    }
    val stale = old.keys.filter { it >= newChunks.size }.map { "$docId:$it" }
    if (stale.isNotEmpty()) store.delete(stale)
    return todo.size to stale.size        // (embedded, deleted)
}
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Function;

public class Sync {
    interface Store {
        Map<Integer, String> getHashes(String docId);
        void upsert(List<Map<String, Object>> items);
        void delete(List<String> ids);
    }

    static String chunkHash(String text) throws Exception {
        String norm = String.join(" ", text.trim().split("\\s+"));
        byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(norm.getBytes("UTF-8"));
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (byte b : d) sb.append(String.format("%02x", b));
        return sb.toString();
    }

    static int[] syncDocument(String docId, List<String> chunks, Store store,
                              Function<List<String>, List<float[]>> embed) throws Exception {
        Map<Integer, String> old = store.getHashes(docId);
        List<Integer> todo = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < chunks.size(); i++)
            if (!chunkHash(chunks.get(i)).equals(old.get(i))) todo.add(i);
        if (!todo.isEmpty()) {
            List<String> texts = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i : todo) texts.add(chunks.get(i));
            List<float[]> vecs = embed.apply(texts);
            List<Map<String, Object>> items = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int n = 0; n < todo.size(); n++) {
                int i = todo.get(n);
                items.add(Map.of("id", docId + ":" + i, "vector", vecs.get(n),
                        "hash", chunkHash(chunks.get(i)), "doc_id", docId, "text", chunks.get(i)));
            }
            store.upsert(items);
        }
        List<String> stale = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i : old.keySet()) if (i >= chunks.size()) stale.add(docId + ":" + i);
        if (!stale.isEmpty()) store.delete(stale);
        return new int[]{todo.size(), stale.size()};   // {embedded, deleted}
    }
}

A known weakness of index-based chunk ids: inserting one paragraph at the top shifts every later chunk index and changes every hash after it, so the whole document re-embeds. Fix with content-defined chunk boundaries (split on headings) or keying by heading path, and accept the cost for plain text.

Production failure patterns.

  • Parser silently failing. The PDF edit arrives but extraction returns empty text; the old chunks stay, new ones never appear. Alert on "document changed but chunk count 0".
  • Embedding model mismatch. New chunks embedded with model v2 and old with v1 in one index: distances are meaningless across models. Store embedding_model in metadata and never mix.
  • Lag nobody measures. Everything "works" yet lag is 6 hours because a dead-letter queue filled up.

Real products. LlamaIndex has document stores with hash-based refresh and refresh_ref_docs (verify current name); LangChain has an indexing API with a record manager that does similar de-duplication and cleanup (verify). Elastic, Vertex AI Search and Azure AI Search offer incremental indexers with change detection (verify per product).

Real life. A librarian who receives a revised edition: she checks the edition number (hash), swaps only the changed pages, and removes the old pages instead of shelving both.

Common interview traps.

  • "Re-index nightly" is a freshness policy of up to 24 hours of staleness; say so, and ask whether the business can accept it.
  • Updates without deletes leave zombie chunks: old and new versions both retrievable and contradicting each other.
  • Hash the normalized text, not the raw bytes, or whitespace changes cause needless re-embedding.
  • Mixed embedding models inside one index silently destroy retrieval quality.

notes.title: Freshness guarantees: SLOs, tombstones, versions and read-your-writes
notes.html:
Plain words. A "guarantee" means a stated promise such as "99% of edits are searchable within 5 minutes" and a way to prove it. Without a measured promise, freshness is a hope.

Define the SLO (service level objective) from the user's point of view. Freshness lag = (time the new text is first retrievable) minus (time the source was edited). Track p50, p95, p99, not only the average. A typical split: policy and legal content p95 under 5 minutes; wiki content p95 under 1 hour; archives nightly.

Probes prove it. A freshness probe writes a tiny canary document containing a unique random token (for example "canary-7f3a91") into the source, then repeatedly queries the production retrieval path until that token comes back, and records the elapsed time. Run one every few minutes per source. This catches every failure mode in the pipeline, including the ones monitoring dashboards miss.

import time, uuid

def freshness_probe(write_to_source, search, timeout_s=600, poll_s=5):
    token = f"canary-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"
    t0 = time.time()
    write_to_source(f"Freshness probe {token}")        # your connector's write call
    while time.time() - t0 < timeout_s:
        hits = search(token, top_k=3)                  # real production retrieval path
        if any(token in h["text"] for h in hits):
            return time.time() - t0                    # lag in seconds, push to metrics
        time.sleep(poll_s)
    return None                                        # breach: page someone
import java.util.UUID

fun freshnessProbe(writeToSource: (String) -> Unit, search: (String, Int) -> List<String>,
                   timeoutS: Long = 600, pollS: Long = 5): Double? {
    val token = "canary-" + UUID.randomUUID().toString().take(8)
    val t0 = System.nanoTime()
    writeToSource("Freshness probe $token")
    while ((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9 < timeoutS) {
        if (search(token, 3).any { it.contains(token) }) return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9
        Thread.sleep(pollS * 1000)
    }
    return null   // SLO breach
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;

public class Probe {
    static Double freshnessProbe(Consumer<String> writeToSource,
                                 BiFunction<String, Integer, List<String>> search,
                                 long timeoutS, long pollS) throws InterruptedException {
        String token = "canary-" + UUID.randomUUID().toString().substring(0, 8);
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        writeToSource.accept("Freshness probe " + token);
        while ((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9 < timeoutS) {
            for (String t : search.apply(token, 3))
                if (t.contains(token)) return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9;
            Thread.sleep(pollS * 1000);
        }
        return null;   // SLO breach
    }
}

Note the probe only works if retrieval can find a rare token: that needs keyword (BM25) search or hybrid, since a pure vector search may not rank a random string. See also 02_Q1 (hybrid search).

Deletes are harder than inserts. A deleted or revoked document must vanish quickly, often faster than the edit SLO, for legal and security reasons.

  • Tombstone: a marker "doc X is deleted at time T" kept in the queue/metadata so late-arriving old events cannot resurrect it.
  • Soft delete + filter: set deleted=true and always filter on it, then physically purge later. Vector stores with approximate indexes (HNSW) often mark deleted vectors and clean them in background compaction, so physical removal can lag (verify per store).
  • Permissions revoked count as deletes for that user: a user removed from a group must stop retrieving the group's documents immediately. See also 03_O1 (security).

Versioning rules. Choose per content type:

  • Latest wins: keep one version per doc_id; simple, best for policies.
  • Time-travel: keep valid_from/valid_to so "what was the rule in March?" works. Needed for legal, finance and audit.

Query-time safeguards: show the document's last_updated next to each citation; if the top chunk is older than a staleness limit for that doc class, add a warning or fall back to a live tool call (an API that reads the source of truth directly). For truly volatile facts (stock price, order status, inventory) do not index them at all; call the system of record as a tool.

Cache invalidation is part of freshness. Semantic caches (return a stored answer for a similar question) and provider prompt caches (reuse a long identical prefix) can serve stale knowledge after the index changed. Tie cache entries to a corpus_version or the doc versions used, and expire them when any cited doc changes.

Re-embedding migrations. To change embedding model or chunking: build a new index (blue), backfill, run the evaluation set, switch traffic alias to it, keep the old index (green) for rollback for some days. During the backfill, keep forwarding live edits to both indexes or you ship a stale new index.

Production failure patterns.

  • Revoked document still retrievable for 20 minutes because the delete queue lagged behind the update queue.
  • Event ordering: "update" processed after "delete" resurrects a deleted doc. Fix with version numbers or tombstones.
  • Cache served the old price for 24 hours after the index was fixed.

Real life. Recalling a product from shelves: removing it from the warehouse database is not enough; you also pull it from the stores' shelves (caches) and keep a record that it was recalled (tombstone) so a late delivery truck does not restock it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "eventually consistent" without a number. Give an SLO and a probe.
  • Ignoring the delete and permission path; that is the one that causes security incidents.
  • Forgetting caches: a fresh index with a stale cache still returns stale answers.
  • Indexing volatile facts that should be tool calls.

notes.title: Citations: what they are and how to make the model produce usable ones
notes.html:
Plain words. A citation tells the reader which source passage supports which statement, so a human can check it. It is useful only if it is specific (a passage, not just a file) and correct (the passage really supports the statement).

Why it exists. Models can state false things fluently. A citation turns "trust me" into "check this". It also enables audits, legal defensibility, and user trust.

Three ways to get citations (weakest to strongest).

  1. Ask in the prompt: give each chunk an id ([1], [2]) and instruct "cite ids after each claim". Cheap, but the model can cite an id that does not support the claim, or an id that does not exist.
  2. Structured output: require JSON where each claim has text and source_ids, plus a verbatim quote copied from the source. The quote makes mechanical verification possible.
  3. Provider-native citations: some APIs return citation spans pointing at passages of provided documents (Anthropic has a citations feature for supplied documents; verify the current request fields in the docs). Native spans reduce invented quotes, but you should still verify.

Prompt assembly pattern. Label each chunk with a stable id and metadata:

<source id="S3" doc="hr-policy-2026.pdf" page="4" updated="2026-10-01">
Employees may carry over at most 5 unused leave days into the next year.
</source>

then ask for output like:

{"answer_parts":[
   {"text":"You can carry over up to 5 days.",
    "source_id":"S3",
    "quote":"carry over at most 5 unused leave days"}]}

Python with the Anthropic SDK (model id from the shared list; verify against the docs):

import json, os
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"])

def answer_with_quotes(question: str, sources: dict[str, str]) -> dict:
    ctx = "\n".join(f'<source id="{sid}">{txt}</source>' for sid, txt in sources.items())
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
        max_tokens=800,
        system=("Answer ONLY from the sources. Reply with JSON: "
                '{"answer_parts":[{"text":str,"source_id":str,"quote":str}],"can_answer":bool}. '
                "quote must be copied verbatim from the cited source. "
                "If sources do not contain the answer, set can_answer=false and answer_parts=[]."),
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"{ctx}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}],
    )
    return json.loads(msg.content[0].text)   # prints e.g. {'answer_parts': [...], 'can_answer': True}

Kotlin and Java use the Java SDK com.anthropic:anthropic-java; the builder style below follows its documented pattern but verify exact class names in the SDK docs. The point is the prompt contract, which is identical.

import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams
import com.anthropic.models.messages.Model   // verify: model id may be passed as a string instead

fun answerWithQuotes(question: String, sources: Map<String, String>): String {
    val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()          // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    val ctx = sources.entries.joinToString("\n") { "<source id=\"${it.key}\">${it.value}</source>" }
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")                       // verify builder overload in SDK docs
        .maxTokens(800)
        .system("Answer ONLY from the sources. Reply JSON with answer_parts[{text,source_id,quote}] and can_answer.")
        .addUserMessage("$ctx\n\nQuestion: $question")
        .build()
    val msg = client.messages().create(params)
    return msg.content().first().text().get().text()     // JSON string; parse with kotlinx.serialization
}
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

public class Cite {
    static String answerWithQuotes(String question, Map<String, String> sources) {
        AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv();   // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        String ctx = sources.entrySet().stream()
            .map(e -> "<source id=\"" + e.getKey() + "\">" + e.getValue() + "</source>")
            .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
        MessageCreateParams params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
            .model("claude-sonnet-5-5")                             // verify in SDK docs
            .maxTokens(800)
            .system("Answer ONLY from the sources. Reply JSON with answer_parts[{text,source_id,quote}] and can_answer.")
            .addUserMessage(ctx + "\n\nQuestion: " + question)
            .build();
        var msg = client.messages().create(params);
        return msg.content().get(0).asText().text();                // JSON string; parse with Jackson
    }
}

Granularity matters. Document-level citations ("hr-policy.pdf") are nearly useless to a reader; passage-level with page or heading and a deep link is the target. Keep doc_id, page, heading_path, char_start, char_end in chunk metadata at ingestion time, otherwise you cannot build precise citations later. See also 01_R1 (ingestion).

Real products. Perplexity (numbered inline sources), Bing Copilot, Google AI Overviews and NotebookLM (passage-linked), and enterprise tools like Glean show sources; legal tools (Harvey, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel; verify) are held to a higher standard because wrong citations have caused real court sanctions in public cases of fabricated case law.

Real life. Footnotes in a textbook: a good one points to page and line; a bad one just says "see library".

Common interview traps.

  • Asking the model for a citation without giving it ids, so it invents plausible-looking titles.
  • Citing at document level only; you cannot verify what you cannot locate.
  • Assuming a provider-native citation feature removes the need to verify; support is not the same as existence.
  • Dropping metadata at ingestion, which makes precise citations impossible afterward.

notes.title: Citation verification: checking the cited source really supports the claim
notes.html:
Plain words. Verification is a second pass that checks each (claim, cited passage) pair. There are two different questions and they need different tools:

  • Existence: did the cited passage actually exist in what we retrieved? (mechanical)
  • Support: does that passage actually back the claim? (semantic)

Layer 1: structural checks (free, fast, run always).

  1. Is source_id one of the ids we sent? If not, the model invented a source.
  2. Was that source actually among the retrieved chunks for this query?
  3. Is the quote a substring of the source text (after normalizing whitespace and case)? Fuzzy match if you allow small edits; compute a ratio and require, say, 0.9 or higher.
  4. Does the claim contain numbers, dates or named entities that appear in the quote? A claim saying "5 days" with a quote about "10 days" is a mismatch caught without any model.

Layer 2: entailment check (costs a model call or a small classifier). Entailment (or NLI, natural language inference) asks: given premise P (the passage), is hypothesis H (the claim) entailed, contradicted, or neutral? Options:

  • A small NLI cross-encoder model (for example DeBERTa-based models fine-tuned on MNLI; verify exact checkpoints) run locally: cheap, a few ms per pair, limited to short text.
  • An LLM judge with a strict rubric using a cheap fast model (such as claude-haiku-5-5): flexible, costs tokens. Ask for supported | partially | not_supported plus the supporting sentence.

Layer 3: coverage and completeness. Check the reverse direction too: sentences in the answer with NO citation (uncited claims) and cited passages that were never used. Metrics: citation precision (share of citations that truly support their claims), citation recall (share of claims that have a supporting citation). These are the "citation accuracy" numbers from 03_O1; here is how to compute them.

Worked example. An answer has 6 factual claims. Four carry citations; 3 of those 4 are verified as supporting.

  • Citation precision = 3 / 4 = 0.75.
  • Citation recall = 3 / 6 = 0.50 (only 3 of 6 claims have a correct supporting citation). Both are bad; a target for a regulated product might be precision above 0.95 and recall above 0.9 (set by risk, not a universal number).
import re
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

def norm(s): return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip().lower()

def verify_part(part: dict, sources: dict[str, str], judge=None) -> dict:
    sid, quote, claim = part["source_id"], part["quote"], part["text"]
    if sid not in sources:
        return {"ok": False, "reason": "unknown_source_id"}
    src = norm(sources[sid]); q = norm(quote)
    if q in src:
        ratio = 1.0
    else:                                         # fuzzy: best window of same length
        w = len(q)
        ratio = max((SequenceMatcher(None, q, src[i:i+w]).ratio()
                     for i in range(0, max(1, len(src) - w + 1), max(1, w // 4))), default=0)
    if ratio < 0.9:
        return {"ok": False, "reason": f"quote_not_found({ratio:.2f})"}
    nums_claim = set(re.findall(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", claim))
    if not nums_claim <= set(re.findall(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", src)):
        return {"ok": False, "reason": "number_not_in_source"}
    if judge:                                     # optional semantic layer: returns 'supported'|'partial'|'unsupported'
        verdict = judge(premise=sources[sid], claim=claim)
        return {"ok": verdict == "supported", "reason": verdict}
    return {"ok": True, "reason": "structural_pass"}   # e.g. {'ok': True, 'reason': 'structural_pass'}
fun norm(s: String) = s.trim().replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ").lowercase()

data class Part(val text: String, val sourceId: String, val quote: String)

fun verifyPart(p: Part, sources: Map<String, String>, judge: ((String, String) -> String)? = null): Pair<Boolean, String> {
    val srcRaw = sources[p.sourceId] ?: return false to "unknown_source_id"
    val src = norm(srcRaw); val q = norm(p.quote)
    // shortcut: exact substring only; add fuzzy matching (e.g. Levenshtein) if quotes are paraphrased
    if (q !in src) return false to "quote_not_found"
    val num = Regex("\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?")
    val inSrc = num.findAll(src).map { it.value }.toSet()
    if (!num.findAll(p.text).map { it.value }.all { it in inSrc }) return false to "number_not_in_source"
    judge?.let { val v = it(srcRaw, p.text); return (v == "supported") to v }
    return true to "structural_pass"
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.BiFunction;
import java.util.regex.*;

public class Verify {
    record Part(String text, String sourceId, String quote) {}

    static String norm(String s) { return s.trim().replaceAll("\\s+", " ").toLowerCase(); }

    static Set<String> numbers(String s) {
        Set<String> out = new HashSet<>();
        Matcher m = Pattern.compile("\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?").matcher(s);
        while (m.find()) out.add(m.group());
        return out;
    }

    static String verifyPart(Part p, Map<String, String> sources, BiFunction<String, String, String> judge) {
        String raw = sources.get(p.sourceId());
        if (raw == null) return "FAIL:unknown_source_id";
        String src = norm(raw);
        // shortcut: exact substring only; add fuzzy matching if quotes may be paraphrased
        if (!src.contains(norm(p.quote()))) return "FAIL:quote_not_found";
        if (!numbers(src).containsAll(numbers(p.text()))) return "FAIL:number_not_in_source";
        if (judge != null) {
            String v = judge.apply(raw, p.text());
            return v.equals("supported") ? "OK" : "FAIL:" + v;
        }
        return "OK:structural_pass";
    }
}

LLM-judge prompt shape (premise first, strict rubric):

Premise (the only allowed evidence):
"""Employees may carry over at most 5 unused leave days."""
Claim: "You can carry over 10 days."
Answer with one word: supported, partial, or unsupported.
A claim is supported only if every part of it follows from the premise alone.
Do not use outside knowledge.

What happens on failure:

  • Drop the claim and regenerate with the failed claim feedback ("S3 does not say 10 days").
  • Show the answer with the unverified claim flagged or removed.
  • If most claims fail, abstain (next sections).

Subtle failure: the passage supports the claim but is the wrong document. For example an outdated version of the policy supports "10 days". Verification against the retrieved set cannot see this; combine with the freshness metadata (is the cited chunk the latest version?).

Cost note. Verification adds a call per claim or one batched call per answer. Batch all (claim, passage) pairs into one judge prompt with small passages (a few hundred tokens each) so the added cost stays a fraction of generation (see the cost section for the arithmetic).

Real products and papers. Research on attributed LLMs and attribution scoring (for example "ALCE" benchmark for citations, and "AIS" attributable-to-identified-sources evaluation; verify exact titles), RAGAS faithfulness, TruLens groundedness, and Vectara's Hughes Hallucination Evaluation Model (HHEM; verify) all implement variants of the support check.

Real life. A fact-checker at a magazine: she does not trust the footnote; she opens the cited book at that page, finds the sentence, and confirms it says what the article claims.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the same model, in the same call, to generate and to verify; it tends to agree with itself. Verify separately and with a stricter prompt or a different model.
  • Checking only that the quote exists, not that it supports the claim (a true quote can be taken out of context or contradicts the claim by negation).
  • Measuring only precision and forgetting uncited claims (recall).
  • Letting the judge see outside knowledge; the premise must be the only evidence.

notes.title: Confidence signals: how a RAG system knows it might be wrong
notes.html:
Plain words. Confidence is an estimate of "how likely is this answer to be correct and grounded". LLMs are not reliable at saying "I am 90% sure" in words; you need signals measured from the pipeline.

Signals, from retrieval to generation.

Signal What it measures Weakness
Top-1 retrieval score How close the best chunk is to the query Scores are not comparable across embedding models or query types
Score gap (top1 minus top2) Is there one clear winner? Multi-chunk answers have no clear winner
Reranker score Cross-encoder relevance, usually better calibrated than raw cosine Needs calibration on your data
Number of chunks above a threshold Coverage Duplicates inflate it
Query-chunk lexical overlap Keywords really present Misses paraphrase
Citation verification pass rate Share of claims with verified support Costs a call
Self-consistency Ask the model several times; do answers agree? Costs N calls; agreement is not truth
Token log-probabilities Model's own per-token likelihood (if the API exposes them; verify availability) Often unavailable, poorly calibrated
Model-stated confidence "Rate 0 to 100" Verbalized confidence is overconfident; use as a weak feature only

Calibration in plain words. A score is calibrated if, among answers with score 0.8, about 80% are really correct. Raw similarity scores almost never behave this way. You make them behave by collecting labelled examples (question, retrieved chunks, human or judge label "answer correct yes/no"), then fitting a small mapping (logistic regression or isotonic regression) from signals to probability of correct.

Worked arithmetic for a calibration bucket. You have 200 labelled questions; 50 have reranker score in [0.6, 0.7); of those 50, 30 were correct. Empirical accuracy for that bucket = 30 / 50 = 0.60. A system that reports "0.65 confidence" there is close; one that reports "0.9" is overconfident by 0.3. Expected calibration error (ECE) averages this gap weighted by bucket size.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# features per question: [top1_rerank, gap_top1_top2, n_chunks_above_0.5, verify_pass_rate]
X = np.array([[0.92, 0.30, 3, 1.0], [0.40, 0.02, 0, 0.0], [0.75, 0.10, 2, 0.8], [0.55, 0.05, 1, 0.5]])
y = np.array([1, 0, 1, 0])               # 1 = answer judged correct and grounded
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)     # tiny demo; use hundreds of labelled rows in practice
p_correct = clf.predict_proba([[0.70, 0.12, 2, 0.9]])[0, 1]
print(round(float(p_correct), 2))        # estimated probability this answer is correct
import kotlin.math.exp

// Logistic scoring with weights trained offline (e.g., in Python) and shipped as config.
data class Signals(val top1: Double, val gap: Double, val nAbove: Int, val verifyRate: Double)

val w = doubleArrayOf(3.1, 2.2, 0.4, 1.8); const val bias = -3.5   // illustrative, not real trained values

fun pCorrect(s: Signals): Double {
    val z = bias + w[0] * s.top1 + w[1] * s.gap + w[2] * s.nAbove + w[3] * s.verifyRate
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-z))        // prints a value in (0,1)
}
public class Confidence {
    record Signals(double top1, double gap, int nAbove, double verifyRate) {}

    // weights trained offline (e.g., in Python) and shipped as config; values below are illustrative
    static final double[] W = {3.1, 2.2, 0.4, 1.8};
    static final double BIAS = -3.5;

    static double pCorrect(Signals s) {
        double z = BIAS + W[0] * s.top1() + W[1] * s.gap() + W[2] * s.nAbove() + W[3] * s.verifyRate();
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + Math.exp(-z));   // value in (0,1)
    }
}

Training is Python-only on purpose (scikit-learn); the JVM side only needs the weights, which keeps the serving path dependency-free.

Distinguish two kinds of "I do not know".

  • Retrieval failure: the answer exists in the corpus but search did not find it. Fix retrieval (hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting).
  • Knowledge gap: the answer is not in the corpus at all. Correct behaviour is to abstain and route the question (log it to find missing documents). The user sees the same "I could not find that", but the fix differs, so log which one it was by testing with a wider retrieval (larger k) on abstained questions offline.

Production failure patterns.

  • Threshold copied from a blog post (for example "cosine 0.8") and the corpus uses a different embedding model, so everything abstains or nothing does.
  • Confidence computed on easy queries during testing; real users ask vague, multi-part or typo-ridden questions.
  • Score drift after switching embedding model silently moves the whole distribution.

Real life. A doctor deciding whether to give an opinion: how clear the test result is (retrieval score), whether two independent tests agree (self-consistency), and whether past opinions like this one were usually right (calibration).

Common interview traps.

  • Asking the model to output a confidence number and trusting it as probability.
  • Using one global cosine threshold across embedding models and query types.
  • Confusing a high retrieval score (relevant text found) with a correct answer (text actually answers it).
  • Skipping calibration data; you need labelled examples from real traffic.

notes.title: Abstention: designing "I do not know" and the gate that triggers it
notes.html:
Plain words. Abstention means the system declines to answer (or answers partially, or escalates to a human) when evidence is too weak. A good abstention policy is a trade-off, not a safety switch: refusing too often makes the product useless; refusing too rarely makes it dangerous.

The decision gate. After retrieval (and optionally after generation plus verification), compute a decision:

retrieve -> rerank -> confidence p
   p >= T_high            -> answer normally with citations
   T_low <= p < T_high    -> answer with caveat, show sources, offer "ask a human"
   p < T_low              -> abstain: "I could not find this in <knowledge base>",
                              suggest rephrase, log the question for the content team

Also abstain (or ask a clarifying question) for: ambiguous questions ("what is the limit?" which limit?), conflicting sources of equal authority, questions requiring data outside scope (medical or legal advice in a non-medical bot), and cases where citation verification fails on most claims.

Choosing T with data (worked example). Hold out 300 labelled questions: 240 answerable, 60 unanswerable. Sweep the threshold and measure:

  • Answer rate on answerable questions (higher is better).
  • False answer rate on unanswerable questions: share where the bot answers anyway (lower is better).
  • Accuracy when answering.

Suppose at T = 0.5: the system answers 225 of 240 answerable (answer rate 225/240 = 0.9375), of which 207 are correct (accuracy 207/225 = 0.92); and answers 24 of 60 unanswerable (false answer rate 24/60 = 0.40). At T = 0.7: answers 190 of 240 (0.79), correct 181 (181/190 = 0.95), unanswerable answered 6 of 60 (0.10). You pick T from business cost: if a wrong answer costs 20 times a missed answer, favour 0.7; for casual FAQ, 0.5 may do. The point is to choose it from a measured curve, not by feel. (All numbers here are made-up illustrations of the method.)

Code: the gate, plus the sweep.

def decide(p: float, t_low=0.45, t_high=0.70) -> str:
    if p >= t_high: return "answer"
    if p >= t_low:  return "answer_with_caveat"
    return "abstain"                          # e.g. decide(0.3) -> 'abstain'

def sweep(rows, thresholds):
    """rows: list of (p, is_answerable, answer_was_correct)."""
    out = []
    for t in thresholds:
        ans = [r for r in rows if r[0] >= t]
        answerable = [r for r in rows if r[1]]
        unans = [r for r in rows if not r[1]]
        out.append({
            "T": t,
            "answer_rate": sum(1 for r in answerable if r[0] >= t) / len(answerable),
            "false_answer_rate": sum(1 for r in unans if r[0] >= t) / len(unans),
            "accuracy_when_answering": (sum(1 for r in ans if r[2]) / len(ans)) if ans else None,
        })
    return out
enum class Decision { ANSWER, ANSWER_WITH_CAVEAT, ABSTAIN }

fun decide(p: Double, tLow: Double = 0.45, tHigh: Double = 0.70) = when {
    p >= tHigh -> Decision.ANSWER
    p >= tLow  -> Decision.ANSWER_WITH_CAVEAT
    else       -> Decision.ABSTAIN
}

data class Row(val p: Double, val answerable: Boolean, val correct: Boolean)
data class Point(val t: Double, val answerRate: Double, val falseAnswerRate: Double, val accuracy: Double?)

fun sweep(rows: List<Row>, ts: List<Double>): List<Point> = ts.map { t ->
    val ans = rows.filter { it.p >= t }
    val a = rows.filter { it.answerable }; val u = rows.filterNot { it.answerable }
    Point(t, a.count { it.p >= t }.toDouble() / a.size, u.count { it.p >= t }.toDouble() / u.size,
          if (ans.isEmpty()) null else ans.count { it.correct }.toDouble() / ans.size)
}
import java.util.*;

public class Gate {
    enum Decision { ANSWER, ANSWER_WITH_CAVEAT, ABSTAIN }

    static Decision decide(double p, double tLow, double tHigh) {
        if (p >= tHigh) return Decision.ANSWER;
        if (p >= tLow) return Decision.ANSWER_WITH_CAVEAT;
        return Decision.ABSTAIN;
    }

    record Row(double p, boolean answerable, boolean correct) {}

    static double[] sweepPoint(List<Row> rows, double t) {   // {answerRate, falseAnswerRate, accuracy}
        long a = rows.stream().filter(Row::answerable).count();
        long u = rows.size() - a;
        long aAns = rows.stream().filter(r -> r.answerable() && r.p() >= t).count();
        long uAns = rows.stream().filter(r -> !r.answerable() && r.p() >= t).count();
        long ans = rows.stream().filter(r -> r.p() >= t).count();
        long ok = rows.stream().filter(r -> r.p() >= t && r.correct()).count();
        return new double[]{ (double) aAns / a, (double) uAns / u, ans == 0 ? Double.NaN : (double) ok / ans };
    }
}

What a good refusal looks like. Specific and helpful: "I could not find the 2026 travel reimbursement limit in the HR policies I can search. The closest document is Travel-Policy-2024 (last updated Mar 2024), which may be outdated. Would you like me to forward this to HR?" Compare with a useless "I do not know." Include: what was searched, the nearest evidence if any, and a next step.

Partial answers. If three of four sub-questions are supported, answer those three and clearly say the fourth was not found. This beats all-or-nothing in most products.

Prompt-level abstention. Add an explicit instruction and a structured field (can_answer: false) so the model has a legal way out; models forced to answer will fabricate. Test it with adversarial questions that sound plausible but are not in the corpus ("What is our parental leave in Mars office?").

Android angle (client side). A mobile app calling your backend proxy should render the three states differently: normal answer, answer with a visible caveat banner, and a "no answer found" card with a Contact support action. Make the abstain state a first-class field in the API response ("status":"abstained"), never a magic string inside the text, so the UI and analytics can handle it. Never put API keys in the app; the confidence gate runs on the server.

Real products. Customer-support bots (Intercom Fin, Zendesk AI agents; verify) are configured with confidence thresholds and handoff-to-human; Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers contextual grounding checks with a threshold (verify current features); research on selective prediction and "abstain" training (R-tuning, "Know what you do not know" style work; verify exact titles) motivate the idea.

Production failure patterns.

  • Over-refusal after a threshold bump: complaints spike because the bot says "not found" for questions it used to answer. Always monitor answer rate next to accuracy.
  • Refusal loop: user rephrases five times, gets the same refusal. Offer escalation after the second refusal.
  • Sycophancy: user insists, "just guess", and the model answers anyway. Keep the gate outside the model so pressure in the chat cannot override it.
  • Abstentions never reviewed: they are the best signal of missing content. Weekly review of the top abstained questions feeds ingestion.

Real life. A good receptionist: "That is not my department; let me connect you to someone who knows" is better than inventing directions to a room that may not exist.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating abstention as a single prompt line instead of a measured gate with thresholds.
  • Optimizing only accuracy-when-answering (which improves by answering less) without tracking answer rate.
  • Letting the LLM alone decide to abstain; combine with retrieval and verification signals.
  • Not distinguishing "not in corpus" from "retrieval missed it".

notes.title: RAG cost breakdown: the three stages and the formulas
notes.html:
Plain words. RAG spends money in three places: ingestion (preparing the corpus, mostly one-time plus updates), retrieval (per query: embed the query, search, rerank), and generation (per query: the LLM reading the retrieved context and writing the answer). Add fixed infrastructure and the optional quality layers (query rewriting, verification, evaluation). See also 03_O1 (it lists the cost components and optimization levers; this section gives the formulas and measurement).

All prices below are placeholders named like P_in so you can plug in your provider's current prices (prices change often: verify on the provider pricing page). The arithmetic is what matters.

Stage 1: ingestion.

  • Parsing and OCR: per page or per document (OCR and layout models can be the surprise line item for scanned PDFs).
  • Chunking: CPU, negligible.
  • Embedding: tokens_total x price_per_token_embed. Tokens total = chunks x average tokens per chunk (add overlap: 50-token overlap on 400-token chunks inflates tokens by about 50/350 = 14%, since each new chunk adds 350 new tokens).
  • Storage: vectors x dimensions x bytes. A float32 vector of 1,024 dimensions = 1,024 x 4 = 4,096 bytes. 1,000,000 chunks = about 4.1 GB of raw vectors, plus the index overhead (HNSW graph commonly adds tens of percent; verify) and the stored text and metadata. Quantization to int8 divides vector bytes by 4; binary quantization by 32 (quality trade-offs apply).
  • Re-ingestion on updates (see the freshness section): changed tokens only.

Stage 2: retrieval (per query).

  • Query embedding: about 20 to 50 query tokens, so tiny.
  • Vector search: compute or memory hours of the store, amortized per query. Managed stores bill by read units or pod hours (verify).
  • Reranker: a cross-encoder scores each (query, chunk) pair. 50 candidates x 400 tokens = 20,000 tokens processed per query by the reranker; hosted rerank APIs usually bill per search or per 1,000 documents (verify). Often the largest retrieval-side cost.
  • Query rewriting or multi-query: an extra small-model call per query.

Stage 3: generation (per query).

  • Input tokens = system prompt + conversation history + retrieved chunks + question. Example: 600 (system) + 800 (history) + 5 chunks x 400 (2,000) + 50 (question) = 3,450 tokens.
  • Output tokens = answer + citations JSON, say 350.
  • Cost = input_tokens x P_in + output_tokens x P_out. Output tokens usually cost several times input tokens per token (verify the ratio on the current pricing page), and generation is usually 70% or more of per-query cost.
  • Prompt caching: a static prefix (system prompt, tool definitions) can be cached by the provider at a discounted read price (verify the discount and the minimum cacheable length). Retrieved chunks vary per query so they cache poorly; place static text first so the prefix stays identical.

Worked example with placeholder prices. Let P_in = $3 / 1M tokens, P_out = $15 / 1M tokens (illustrative, not a quote), rerank $2 / 1,000 searches, query embedding negligible.

  • Generation: input 3,450 x $3 / 1,000,000 = $0.010350; output 350 x $15 / 1,000,000 = $0.005250; sum = $0.015600.
  • Rerank: $2 / 1,000 = $0.002000.
  • Query rewrite with a small model: say 300 in / 60 out tokens at $0.25 / $1.25 per 1M: 300 x 0.25 / 1M = $0.000075; 60 x 1.25 / 1M = $0.000075; sum = $0.000150.
  • Verification (batched judge, small model): 6 claims x 300 tokens = 1,800 in plus 100 out: 1,800 x 0.25 / 1M = $0.000450; 100 x 1.25 / 1M = $0.000125; sum = $0.000575.
  • Per-query variable cost = 0.015600 + 0.002000 + 0.000150 + 0.000575 = $0.018325, about 1.8 cents.
  • At 100,000 queries a month: 100,000 x 0.018325 = $1,832.50 per month, plus fixed infrastructure.
  • Generation share = 0.0156 / 0.018325 = 85%. Verification adds 0.000575 / 0.018325 = about 3%: cheap relative to generation, so verifying is rarely the cost problem; the 5 retrieved chunks and long history are.

Ingestion for the same system (1,000,000 chunks x 450 effective tokens = 450,000,000 tokens; at a placeholder embed price of $0.10 / 1M) = 450 x $0.10 = $45 one-time. This illustrates a common surprise: ingestion is often tiny versus months of generation.

cost per answer
  = embed_q + search + rerank + rewrite            (retrieval side)
  + (in_tokens x P_in) + (out_tokens x P_out)      (generation)
  + verify                                         (optional)
cost per month = cost per answer x queries + ingestion_updates + fixed infra

Where money really leaks.

  • Retrieving k = 20 chunks "for safety": 20 x 400 = 8,000 input tokens instead of 2,000: generation input cost quadruples for marginal quality.
  • Conversation history resent in full every turn: it grows linearly, so total tokens across a conversation grow roughly quadratically.
  • Retries and timeouts re-paying for the same call.
  • Evaluation runs: an LLM-judge over 1,000 test questions after every change adds up; run the full suite nightly, a small smoke set per commit.
  • Idle vector store capacity sized for peak.

Real products. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google bill by input and output tokens and expose usage in every response; Cohere, Voyage and Jina offer rerank APIs; pgvector avoids a separate store bill; LangSmith, Langfuse and Helicone capture token and cost per trace (verify features).

Real life. A restaurant's cost per dish: ingredients (generation) dominate, but the prep chef's time (retrieval) and the one-time kitchen setup (ingestion) also count, and the accountant needs all three on one sheet.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting only the model price and forgetting the reranker, rewriter, verifier and eval runs.
  • Forgetting that output tokens are priced higher than input tokens.
  • Ignoring history growth in multi-turn chats.
  • Calling ingestion the main cost; for a read-heavy product it is usually the smallest line over a year.

notes.title: Measuring cost in production: a per-request meter and attribution
notes.html:
Plain words. You cannot reduce what you cannot see. Cost measurement means attaching a small record to every request that says how many tokens and how much money each stage used, then aggregating by feature, tenant and outcome.

What to record per request (one structured log line or trace span per stage).

  • request_id, tenant_id, feature, corpus_version, model.
  • Per stage: latency ms, input tokens, output tokens, cached input tokens, number of retrieved chunks, retries.
  • Outcome: answered / caveat / abstained, citation precision (if verified), user feedback.
  • Computed cost_usd from a versioned price table (prices change; store the table version on each record).

Two metrics that matter more than the total.

  • Cost per answered question and cost per successful (helpful) answer: an abstained query still costs retrieval plus the gate. Note: total spend / answered count is a different number from spend / total count; report both.
  • Cost per tenant: needed for pricing plans and spotting one noisy customer.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

PRICES = {  # USD per 1M tokens; PLACEHOLDERS, load the real table from config (verify provider pricing)
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": {"in": 3.00, "out": 15.00, "cached_in": 0.30},
    "claude-haiku-5-5":  {"in": 0.25, "out": 1.25,  "cached_in": 0.03},
}

@dataclass
class CostMeter:
    request_id: str
    stages: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

    def add_llm(self, stage, model, tin, tout, cached=0):
        p = PRICES[model]
        usd = ((tin - cached) * p["in"] + cached * p["cached_in"] + tout * p["out"]) / 1e6
        self.stages[stage] = self.stages.get(stage, 0.0) + usd

    def add_flat(self, stage, usd):            # rerank per-search fee, vector store read units, etc.
        self.stages[stage] = self.stages.get(stage, 0.0) + usd

    def total(self): return sum(self.stages.values())

m = CostMeter("req-1")
m.add_llm("generate", "claude-sonnet-5-5", tin=3450, tout=350)
m.add_flat("rerank", 0.002)
print(round(m.total(), 6), m.stages)     # 0.0176 {'generate': 0.0156, 'rerank': 0.002}
data class Price(val inP: Double, val outP: Double, val cachedIn: Double)   // USD per 1M tokens; placeholders

val PRICES = mapOf(
    "claude-sonnet-5-5" to Price(3.00, 15.00, 0.30),
    "claude-haiku-5-5" to Price(0.25, 1.25, 0.03),
)

class CostMeter(val requestId: String) {
    val stages = mutableMapOf<String, Double>()

    fun addLlm(stage: String, model: String, tin: Int, tout: Int, cached: Int = 0) {
        val p = PRICES.getValue(model)
        val usd = ((tin - cached) * p.inP + cached * p.cachedIn + tout * p.outP) / 1e6
        stages.merge(stage, usd, Double::plus)
    }

    fun addFlat(stage: String, usd: Double) { stages.merge(stage, usd, Double::plus) }
    fun total() = stages.values.sum()     // 0.0176 after the two calls in the Python example
}
import java.util.*;

public class CostMeter {
    record Price(double in, double out, double cachedIn) {}   // USD per 1M tokens; placeholders

    static final Map<String, Price> PRICES = Map.of(
        "claude-sonnet-5-5", new Price(3.00, 15.00, 0.30),
        "claude-haiku-5-5", new Price(0.25, 1.25, 0.03));

    final String requestId;
    final Map<String, Double> stages = new LinkedHashMap<>();

    CostMeter(String requestId) { this.requestId = requestId; }

    void addLlm(String stage, String model, int tin, int tout, int cached) {
        Price p = PRICES.get(model);
        double usd = ((tin - cached) * p.in() + cached * p.cachedIn() + tout * p.out()) / 1e6;
        stages.merge(stage, usd, Double::sum);
    }

    void addFlat(String stage, double usd) { stages.merge(stage, usd, Double::sum); }

    double total() { return stages.values().stream().mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue).sum(); }
}

Token counts come from the provider response (every major API returns a usage object with input and output tokens; field names differ per provider, verify). Do not estimate with word counts if you can read the real usage.

Attribution rules.

  • Shared costs (vector store, always-on servers) are allocated by query share or storage share per tenant; document the rule.
  • Tag evaluation and backfill traffic with purpose=eval or purpose=ingest so dashboards separate production spend from engineering spend.
  • Retried calls: log each attempt; a hidden retry storm doubles cost.

Budgets and guardrails.

  • Per-request token cap (limit retrieved context and max_tokens).
  • Per-tenant daily budget with graceful degradation (smaller model, fewer chunks) rather than hard failure.
  • Anomaly alert: cost per request rises more than 30% week over week (a typical starting alert; tune).
  • Cost-quality curves: when testing "cheaper" settings (k from 8 to 4, smaller model), compare quality metrics on the eval set alongside cost per answer. A saving that drops groundedness by 8 points may cost more in support tickets.

Android angle. Mobile clients should never compute or hold prices or keys. Send only the user question to your backend; the backend logs cost. If you show quota to users ("12 of 50 questions left"), enforce it server-side. On-device models (Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI, MediaPipe LLM Inference) have no per-token fee but cost latency, battery and quality; a hybrid router that answers short, simple questions on device and sends the rest to the server is a real cost lever (verify device support).

Production failure patterns.

  • Cost dashboards built from the provider invoice only: delayed by a day and impossible to split by feature.
  • Price table hard-coded in code and stale after a provider price change; version the table.
  • One tenant pasting 200-page documents into the chat drives 60% of spend; no per-tenant cap existed.
  • Caching disabled by accident because a timestamp in the system prompt made every prefix unique.

Real life. A taxi meter: it runs per ride, itemizes the fare, and lets the company see which routes and which drivers cost what, instead of reviewing only the monthly fuel bill.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating tokens from characters instead of reading the API usage field.
  • Reporting average cost only; p95 and the most expensive 1% of requests reveal the real problems.
  • Forgetting to separate eval and ingestion spend from serving spend.
  • Cutting cost without re-running the quality evaluation.

notes.title: Putting it together: one request, end to end
notes.html:
Plain words. Here is the whole flow in the order a request experiences it, so the four ideas connect.

user question
  1. router: needs retrieval? (small talk -> skip, saves cost)
  2. rewrite (optional, small model)                            [cost meter]
  3. hybrid retrieve + metadata/ACL filter                      [freshness: only live, latest, permitted chunks]
  4. rerank -> confidence signals (scores, gap)                 [cost meter]
  5. gate #1: p < T_low -> abstain (skip generation entirely)   [saves the biggest cost]
  6. generate with ids + verbatim quotes, can_answer field      [cost meter]
  7. verify citations (structural, then entailment)             [cost meter]
  8. gate #2: too many failed claims -> regenerate once or abstain
  9. respond: answer + passage-level citations + last_updated dates + status field
 10. log trace: request_id, corpus_version, scores, verdicts, cost, outcome

Observations worth stating in an interview:

  • Gate #1 is a cost feature: abstaining before generation spends only retrieval money. If 15% of traffic is out of scope, that avoids 15% of the most expensive stage.
  • Freshness metadata flows into the answer: showing "updated 2026-10-01" next to a citation lets the user judge staleness, and the verifier can reject a citation to a superseded version.
  • One trace id ties everything: when a user reports a wrong answer, you can see which chunks were retrieved, whether the corpus version was current, how the verifier voted, and what the request cost.
  • Regeneration is capped (once) so a failing question cannot loop and burn tokens.

A minimal orchestrator sketch in Python (the three stages are stubs for the functions built earlier):

def handle(question, retrieve, generate, verify_all, confidence, meter):
    chunks = retrieve(question)                          # filtered to live, latest, permitted chunks
    p = confidence(chunks)
    if p < 0.45:
        return {"status": "abstained", "reason": "low_retrieval_confidence"}
    out = generate(question, chunks, meter)              # JSON with answer_parts and can_answer
    if not out["can_answer"]:
        return {"status": "abstained", "reason": "model_no_answer"}
    verdicts = [verify_all(part, chunks) for part in out["answer_parts"]]
    ok_rate = sum(v["ok"] for v in verdicts) / max(1, len(verdicts))
    if ok_rate < 0.8:
        return {"status": "abstained", "reason": f"citation_check_failed({ok_rate:.2f})"}
    return {"status": "answered", "parts": out["answer_parts"], "cost_usd": meter.total()}
fun handle(
    question: String,
    retrieve: (String) -> List<String>,
    generate: (String, List<String>) -> List<Part>?,      // null = model said it cannot answer
    verify: (Part, List<String>) -> Boolean,
    confidence: (List<String>) -> Double,
    meter: CostMeter,
): Map<String, Any> {
    val chunks = retrieve(question)
    if (confidence(chunks) < 0.45) return mapOf("status" to "abstained", "reason" to "low_retrieval_confidence")
    val parts = generate(question, chunks) ?: return mapOf("status" to "abstained", "reason" to "model_no_answer")
    val okRate = parts.count { verify(it, chunks) }.toDouble() / maxOf(1, parts.size)
    if (okRate < 0.8) return mapOf("status" to "abstained", "reason" to "citation_check_failed")
    return mapOf("status" to "answered", "parts" to parts, "cost_usd" to meter.total())
}
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;

public class Pipeline {
    record Part(String text, String sourceId, String quote) {}

    static Map<String, Object> handle(String question,
                                      Function<String, List<String>> retrieve,
                                      BiFunction<String, List<String>, List<Part>> generate, // null = cannot answer
                                      BiPredicate<Part, List<String>> verify,
                                      ToDoubleFunction<List<String>> confidence,
                                      Supplier<Double> costSoFar) {
        List<String> chunks = retrieve.apply(question);
        if (confidence.applyAsDouble(chunks) < 0.45)
            return Map.of("status", "abstained", "reason", "low_retrieval_confidence");
        List<Part> parts = generate.apply(question, chunks);
        if (parts == null) return Map.of("status", "abstained", "reason", "model_no_answer");
        long ok = parts.stream().filter(p -> verify.test(p, chunks)).count();
        if ((double) ok / Math.max(1, parts.size()) < 0.8)
            return Map.of("status", "abstained", "reason", "citation_check_failed");
        return Map.of("status", "answered", "parts", parts, "cost_usd", costSoFar.get());
    }
}

Production failure patterns across the whole flow.

  • Verifier and generator disagree on formatting (curly quotes, soft hyphens from PDF extraction): quotes fail verification though the claim is right. Normalize unicode at ingestion and in the verifier.
  • Layers add latency: rerank + generation + verification can double time to first token if verification blocks streaming. Stream the answer and verify asynchronously for low-risk products; block on verification for regulated ones.
  • Thresholds frozen forever while the corpus and models change; re-run the sweep after every embedding model, reranker or prompt change.

Real life. An airport: check-in (retrieval), security (verification), a gate agent who can say "this flight does not exist" (abstention), and a fuel and staffing ledger for each flight (cost), all working off the same boarding record (trace).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing the layers without saying where they run in the order; abstaining before generation is the cost-saving placement.
  • Blocking every request on verification regardless of risk level, destroying latency.
  • Leaving thresholds untuned after changing models or corpus.
  • Not returning a machine-readable status, so clients and analytics cannot tell abstentions from answers.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Freshness. Freshness is lag between source edit and retrievable text, so define it as an SLO (for example p95 under N minutes), measure it with canary probes that query the real retrieval path, and make the pipeline incremental and idempotent: detect change (webhook or diff), hash normalized chunk text, embed only changed chunks (hashing cuts a 2%-daily-change corpus re-embed cost by 50x in the worked example), upsert with deterministic ids, and delete stale chunks. Deletes and permission revocations need tombstones and faster targets than edits; caches must be invalidated by corpus version; never mix embedding models in one index; migrate with blue/green indexes. Volatile facts belong behind tool calls, not in the index.

Citations. Make citations passage-level and verifiable by labelling chunks with ids and requiring a verbatim quote per claim (or using provider-native citation features, verify in docs). Verify in layers: structural (known id, quote is a substring, numbers match), semantic (NLI or a strict LLM judge using the passage as the only evidence), then coverage (citation precision and recall; the worked example gives 3/4 = 0.75 precision and 3/6 = 0.50 recall). Verify with a separate call, check version freshness, and on failure drop, regenerate once, or abstain.

Confidence and abstention. Raw scores are not probabilities; combine signals (rerank score, gap, evidence count, verification pass rate, self-consistency) and calibrate them on labelled traffic. Build a three-way gate (answer, answer with caveat, abstain) and choose thresholds from a sweep of answer rate, false-answer rate and accuracy-when-answering on answerable and unanswerable questions. Write helpful refusals, support partial answers, keep the gate outside the model, return a machine-readable status, separate "not in corpus" from "retrieval missed it", and review abstained questions to find missing content. Abstaining before generation also saves the costliest stage.

RAG cost. Cost per answer = retrieval (query embed, search, rerank, rewrite) + generation (input tokens x price_in + output tokens x price_out) + optional verification; monthly cost adds ingestion updates and fixed infrastructure. In the worked example, 3,450 input and 350 output tokens at placeholder prices gave $0.0156 generation, $0.018325 per query in total (generation about 85%), $1,832.50 per 100,000 queries, against a one-time ingestion of $45 for 450M tokens (all prices placeholders: verify). Meter every stage per request with versioned prices, read real usage fields, split eval and ingest spend from serving, track cost per answered question, per tenant and p95, cap k and history, keep static prefixes cache-friendly, and re-run quality evaluation whenever a cost optimization is applied.

Interview one-liners. "Freshness is an SLO measured by canary probes, not a nightly job." "A citation is only worth something if verified: existence first, support second, coverage third." "Abstention is a calibrated threshold chosen from a sweep, placed before generation." "Cost is per-stage and per-request; ingestion is usually the smallest line, generation the largest."
